newsitem.title: VATICAN: Vatican says young being turned off religious life.
newsitem.headline: Vatican says young being turned off religious life.

text.p: Young people are reluctant to devote their lives to the Roman Catholic Church because of increasing materialism, broken homes and the demands of celibacy, the Vatican said on Tuesday.

"Secularism and materialism, dominant in the culture of contemporary society, have led to the diminution of the moral sense and the fragility of the life of faith," the Pontifical Work for Ecclesiastical Vocations said in a new document.

The report, prepared with information from Church leaders across Europe ahead of a congress on vocations to be held in Rome next May, found the total number of priests had fallen by nearly 13 percent between 1978 and 1994.

The number of ordinations rose 37 percent over the period, with 2,479 people ordained in 1994. But they were being fast outstripped by the number of priests dying or leaving the priesthood -- a total of 3,686 in 1994.
The report said the number of women in religious orders across Europe fell 24 percent between 1978 and 1994 to 414,687.
"We're touching a nerve that is very important for the Church," Cardinal Pio Laghi, president of the Pontifical Work for Ecclesiastical Vocations, told a news conference.
"We're a bit in crisis in Europe."
He said the Church should not change its policy, but should "train the trainers" and underline its commitment to principles.
"The problem today in this kind of society...(is) a problem of a crisis of values, of principles," he said.
The document said many young people lacked discipline for the difficulties of a priestly life and noted that many new recruits gave up at the first sign of difficulty.

"The situation of broken families, the reduced number of children and the obstacles which even Christian families place in the way of the choice to 'radically follow' the Lord, have become conditions which mitigate against the growth and support and encouragement of vocations," it said.
Belgian, Swiss and Scandinavian Church leaders were among those in the report to highlight "in the obligation of celibacy a negative obstacle to vocations".

Pope John Paul insists clerics must remain chaste but a string of lurid sex scandals, including the case of a Scottish bishop who ran off with one woman last month 15 years after fathering a love child with another, has prompted many to wonder whether the Church should not relax the ruling.
Laghi said prevalent social attitudes created a mentality that had to be changed.
"Scandinavia -- you know what kind of society there is there," he said. "There is no limit to freedom. Life is too easy...it's not so easy to cultivate vocations."
The document also found that some religious communities were at fault for not promoting the priesthood or doing enough to reflect on women's place in the Church.
"In general there does not appear to be a sensitivity on the part of bishops and parish priests towards promotion of vocations to the religious life," the document said.
Next year's congress will tackle how to address the twin problems of attracting new recruits and an ageing priestly population.
"The Church must be able to welcome young people and discern the signs of newness and hope," it said.
